item.title: Marsha Blackburn Offers No Apology Over Kendrick Lamar AI Clip
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Marsha Blackburn's Kendrick Lamar AI defense came months after she demanded the removal of an AI attack ad targeting her.
item.content:encoded:
Marsha Blackburn said she never meant to offend Black Americans with her campaign’s AI remake of Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl performance, offering a new defense without an apology.

The Tennessee Republican faced a direct question about that criticism when FOX13 reporter Rob Sneed caught up with her after a public safety roundtable in Shelby County on Friday. He also asked whether she understood the song’s lyrics and the reaction to the clip.

“We, there would never be any action that was intended to offend,” Blackburn said.

She again credited a county commissioner with making the video and said her campaign shared it because she thought it was fun. Her campaign’s stated priorities included affordability and public safety, alongside education, health care and infrastructure.

The answer added to a dispute that began when Blackburn posted the clip October 13 to promote early voting in her run for governor. The AI scene put her in Kendrick Lamar’s place and turned fellow Tennessee Republicans into dancers as “Not Like Us” played.

Her Democratic opponent, Jerri Green, had already criticized the use of AI in the campaign. Blackburn’s earlier description of the post as a “funsie” also preceded the new question about Black Americans who found it offensive.

The controversy touches a cause Blackburn has championed in Washington: protecting people from digital copies made without their consent. In June, she and Chris Coons announced that their NO FAKES proposal had cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee. Her office described safeguards for voices and visual likenesses, with exceptions for protected speech.

Blackburn had also sought protection from AI campaign content herself. In July, she demanded that the American Exceptionalism Institute PAC remove an AI attack ad within 48 hours and disclose its use of the technology, WPLN reported.

That ad accused her of taking drug-industry money in exchange for legislation. Her letter denied that she ever accepted a bribe to pass a bill. The two disputes involved different uses of AI: one made an allegation against Blackburn, while her post recast a music performance as a voting pitch. Her spokesperson told WPLN that two TV stations had pulled the attack ad.

item.title: 50 Cent Slams The Door On Courtney Kemp As “Power” Creator Hits Back
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: 50 Cent ruled out another Courtney Kemp project as the "Power" creator disputed his claims about their hit TV partnership.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent ruled out working with Courtney Kemp again, and the “Power” creator pushed back on his claims about their work.

“I don’t look forward to working with her ever again,” he told Variety in a new interview.

The rapper felt Kemp had lost sight of his role in selling the show. He pointed to the music he made for pitches and his work to get the series off the ground.

Kemp challenged his budget claims and his grasp of how the show was run. She also denied that she had played down his part in its success.

“I have never once understated his importance in the genesis of ‘Power,'” she said.

Their roles were clear when Starz first picked up the show in 2013. Kemp created the crime drama and took on the job of showrunner, while 50 joined as an executive producer. The network’s first order was for eight episodes.

That grew into a much bigger deal. The first “Power” ran for six seasons and ended in 2020. Its spinoffs kept key characters on screen as the show branched out into a string of new stories.

Music was part of the show’s sound from the start. 50’s “Big Rich Town” video, with Joe, came out in April 2014 before the show’s debut. Starz also offered the video as a first-season bonus.

In 2021, Kemp signed a Netflix deal and passed the day-to-day work on “Power Book II: Ghost” to Brett Mahoney before its third season. She kept an executive producer role in the “Power” shows.

Her move to a new home for her own shows came years before this latest clash over credit. Both Kemp and 50 still had executive producer credits for that third season of “Ghost.”

Kemp went on to create “Nemesis” with Tani Marole. The eight-part Netflix crime drama came out in May and followed a Los Angeles cop and a master thief. It was the first show from her deal with the streamer. Netflix ordered a second season in June.

The work she and 50 built together also found a new home. A Netflix rights deal included U.S. rights to the original “Power” and international rights to its first four series, with the rollout set for November.

Kemp said she had moved on in her career and hoped 50’s “Street Fighter” success would help him do the same.

item.title: Eminem Defends Kid Rock Collab With Message About Their Friendship
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Eminem explained why he teamed with Kid Rock as their new song put a long friendship back under the glare of political debate.
item.content:encoded:
Eminem defended his new song with Kid Rock on October 17. He said an old friendship brought them back together despite the clash over their politics.

The rapper shared his stance on X as “Heal My Faith” arrived on Rock’s new Christian album, “Halfway 2 Jesus.”

He wrote, “Not about choosing sides, just choosing to make music with my old friend. Praying for all of us.”

His post tagged Kid Rock and used the song’s hashtag. It put the focus on their bond after weeks of debate over the pairing.

Rock backs Donald Trump. Eminem has long criticized him. He appeared at a Detroit rally for Kamala Harris in October 2024. He urged the crowd to vote before he brought former President Barack Obama to the stage.

At that event, he also spoke about the right to express one’s views without fear of payback. Obama then walked out to “Lose Yourself” and rapped part of the hit.

Kid Rock told Fox News this month that he and Eminem had refused to let politics break their friendship.

The new statement follows a change in the album’s guest list. AllHipHop reported that Rock posted a new tracklist on October 14. It put Lil Wayne on “7 Sins,” where fans had first expected to hear Eminem.

That change did not mean Eminem had left the project. Rock kept him on the fifth track, “Heal My Faith,” while Wayne took the third slot. Rock used a video to spell out the switch for fans who had objected to the joint record.

Their ties stretch back well before this dispute. Eminem appeared on “F#ck Off” from Rock’s 1998 album “Devil Without A Cause.” Rock later made a cameo in Eminem’s “Berzerk” video.

Consequence reports that the new song reaches back to one of Rock’s early shows of support. In his verse, Eminem recalls Rock attending the release party for “The Slim Shady EP” while he was still unknown. He casts their bond as one that can survive how each man votes. Rock ends the track with a spoken message about their friendship and the freedom to hold different views.

item.title: MGK’s Car At Dakota Johnson’s House Adds To Dating Buzz
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: MGK and Dakota Johnson left an LA studio together as photos of his car at her home added to weeks of dating speculation.
item.content:encoded:
Machine Gun Kelly and Dakota Johnson left a Los Angeles studio together on October 15, adding a late-night stop to the outings that have fueled dating rumors.

Page Six, in a report carried by AOL, said Johnson waited outside while the rapper finished a recording session. She wore a leopard-print coat and held what appeared to be a laptop.

When MGK came out, he moved a bag from the front seat into his trunk. Johnson then got into his Maserati, and the pair left together.

The next morning, his car remained parked at Johnson’s home, the account said. The outlet described the outing as an apparent overnight stay based on photos of the vehicle outside her house.

The pair had also stepped out at Hollywood’s Say Yes lounge earlier in the week, extending a run of sightings that began drawing attention in September.

Us Weekly traced their New York outing to September 11, when they visited Taylor Swift’s Tribeca apartment before going to dinner at Estela. An unnamed source described the visit as a date and said Swift had offered the space because the two wanted privacy.

They had also attended Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July, which sources pointed to as the start of their connection.

Later in September, another source described them as “seriously dating” and said they had kept in touch daily. Johnson also attended the Vogue World: Milano show, where MGK walked the runway on September 22.

The sightings followed high-profile breakups for both stars. MGK and Megan Fox split in late 2024, while Johnson’s eight-year relationship with Coldplay frontman Chris Martin ended in 2025. She later dated singer Role Model before their split this summer.

Johnson addressed the rush to label her outings during a September appearance on Vogue’s “The Run-Through” podcast. She said even dinner with her manager or lawyer could trigger headlines about a mystery man. Asked whether she wanted to correct such stories, she said she preferred to put her energy elsewhere.

“People are gonna believe what they wanna believe, and I don’t have the energy to fight for that,” Johnson said.

item.title: DDG & PlaqueBoyMax Face Off For Best Music Streamer At 2026 Streamer Awards
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: DDG and PlaqueBoyMax joined a four-way music race, with fans holding most of the vote before the November ceremony.
item.content:encoded:
DDG and PlaqueBoyMax landed nominations for Best Music Streamer at the 2026 Streamer Awards. The ballot put two creators who make records in front of their audiences in the same race.

Bishu and AriAtHome rounded out the four-person field on the official ballot. Voting opened October 16, with the show set for November 12.

Organizers described the music award as a prize for a “Streamer who creates the best music content, showcasing talents such as singing, playing instruments, DJing, producing, composing, or more.”

For DDG, the nomination followed another round of making an album live. He released the 15-track “HIT-A-THON” last month after a seven-day, around-the-clock stream in Atlanta. Viewers watched the recording process as guests came through to work on songs.

The finished project included Lil Yachty, 42 Dugg and Real Boston Richey, carrying those on-camera sessions into an album released through Epic Records.

His 2025 “Hit-A-Thon” gave viewers a say in the songs that made the record. They also had input on the beats and offered feedback on his lyrics. Shaboozey, Kevin Gates and Ty Dolla $ign were among the artists who joined him.

In a 2025 Billboard interview, DDG said the format let fans follow his studio work and see his first meetings with guest artists. He said that access helped viewers feel involved.

PlaqueBoyMax’s viewers also had a role in the songs he made with guest artists. His chat helped choose names for new tracks, a part of his process that Boardroom explored in a June profile and interview. The audience could follow a song through a live session as the work took shape in his studio.

His work also reached the Grammys. “Victory Lap,” his collaboration with Fred again.. and Skepta, earned a Best Dance/Electronic Recording nomination at this year’s ceremony. The Recording Academy listed PlaqueBoyMax among the song’s producers as well as its artists.

The Streamer Awards let creators put themselves up for an award for the first time this year. QTCinderella said fans’ top picks would fill each race, with a panel adding one more name.

Fans will account for 70% of the final result, while the panel will supply the other 30%. Voting closes October 31.

item.title: Meagan Good Bet On 50 Cent After Missing Busta Rhymes’ Call
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Meagan Good recalled missing a Busta Rhymes video call before choosing 50 Cent's "21 Questions" to reshape her career.
item.content:encoded:
Meagan Good missed a call about starring in a Busta Rhymes video, then bet on 50 Cent to help audiences see her as a grown woman.

In a new SiriusXM FLY interview, Good told host Eutopia she was disappointed about losing the Busta opportunity. Her mother told her to check her messages. When “21 Questions” came along, her manager had doubts about 50 Cent’s image. Good recalled pushing back and seeing a chance to change her own.

“I was like to me, this is a national commercial,” she said.

Her plan hinged on how people would encounter the video. A movie or TV show needed viewers to choose it; a music video could keep reaching them through repeat plays. She wanted that exposure to mark her move from child actor to adult roles.

That struggle had started well before the shoot. In an earlier Composure interview, Good described career doubts at 19 as she tried to make that shift. She said her faith helped her decide to keep acting and use the platform to encourage young women. The issue also shaped how she dressed: as she got older, she wanted her look to show that she was no longer a child.

The role arrived during 50 Cent’s breakout year. “21 Questions,” featuring Nate Dogg, spent four weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in 2003. “In Da Club” had already taken him to the top. On “Get Rich Or Die Tryin’,” the love song offered another side of the rapper who had built his name on street tales and sharp attacks on rivals.

Good played his partner in a video that put 50 Cent behind bars and cast Tyson Beckford as a rival inmate. The jail visits and calls made their relationship the center of the clip, giving her a role in its story.

Changing her image was one step; gaining control over the roles available to women was another. By 2015, Good and Tamara Bass were creating their own work through Krazy Actress Productions and the web series “All That Matters.”

Good told AllHipHop that women on screen were too often love interests or victims, with other kinds of characters pushed out of the lead. She and Bass wanted stories that gave women their own views, flaws and lives. The project let them pursue those ideas from behind the camera, rather than wait for someone else to offer them a part.

The full interview was scheduled to start streaming on SiriusXM’s app October 14 at 4 P.M. ET.

item.title: Kash’s Father Urges Public To Stop Hate Toward Sister Charged In Her Death
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Kash’s father called for compassion toward the sister charged in her death and shared her plans for a life beyond reality TV.
item.content:encoded:
Kash’s father urged people to stop directing hate at the sister charged in her death as his family mourned the reality star.

Mack Paige Jr. spoke with KRON4 about losing his daughter, Mackayla “Kash” Paige. He asked for compassion toward her sister, Vernika Dunbar, while pushing back on strangers turning the family’s loss into social media content.

The appeal came after Dunbar was charged with involuntary manslaughter. Oakland police alleged that the 38-year-old tried to strike another woman with a gun during a fight involving Kash, but the weapon fired and hit her sister.

Dunbar also faced assault with a firearm and gun charges. Police said the assault charge concerned the alleged attempt to hit the other woman with the gun.

Officers responded near 14th and Harrison streets in downtown Oakland around 1:30 a.m. October 11. They tried to save the 29-year-old’s life before she was taken to a hospital, where she died. Police had not explained what started the confrontation in their account of the charges.

Paige also described plans his daughter had been making beyond the reality-TV spotlight. He said Kash wanted a break and hoped to pursue work as a makeup artist. His account added to what relatives had shared about her hopes before her death.

At a memorial, her cousin Azima King told ABC7 that Kash had wanted to change her life.

“She just wanted better for her life. And she wanted to be better. And she wanted to change,” King said.

Kash had built a following through Now That’s TV, which confirmed her death and shared a tribute. But her father said the attention that followed her screen persona had also brought threats in public. He objected to people discussing the fatal encounter as though they knew what happened when they had not been there.

Dr. Donnetrice Allison, a Stockton University researcher who studies Black women on reality TV, told ABC7 that she worried about the pressure to turn physical clashes into entertainment and chase attention online.

Paige said the family appreciated the support coming its way, while asking for privacy and patience from people expecting a response as they mourned.

item.title: Lil Baby Plans Charity Shift Toward Jobs And Schools After Millions In Giveaways
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Lil Baby's next charity plans focus on jobs and schools, building on years of giveaways and a $150,000 scholarship fund.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Baby plans to steer his nonprofit toward jobs and school support, telling Jaylen Brown he wants the millions he spends on Atlanta giveaways to have a lasting effect on young people.

In “The Last Ten,” released October 16 by Glass Window Productions, he said he told his team “this year is my last time doing that” while discussing his back-to-school and Christmas drives.

Lil Baby wants to work directly with schools and school boards, create “real jobs” and give young people places to go. He used $100,000 as an example of money that could change a system once he understood how it worked.

He wants young people to still point to the help 20 years later. Brown agreed, urging people with money and influence to change the systems that leave families in need.

His current giving includes the sixth annual Back to School Fest, which served 4,000 Atlanta students on July 25 at West End Production Park.

Lil Baby and The Jones Project provided free school supplies, clothing, uniforms, haircuts, food and gift cards, WSB-TV reported.

Families also had games and other activities, with support from partners including The Athlete’s Foot, Fanatics and Dr. Bombay.

At the festival, Lil Baby spent the day meeting children and parents. His earlier community work also includes fixing up basketball courts at Oakland City Park, donating shoes, bicycles and winter coats, and helping pay students’ college tuition.

Education has been part of that work for years. In March 2020, he announced a $150,000 endowed scholarship fund at Booker T. Washington High School, which he once attended. The “My Turn” awards were meant for students who showed excellence and leadership in class.

Atlanta Public Schools officials said the first scholarship went to a senior bound for Dartmouth College, where he planned to play football. The amount of that first award was not disclosed.

At the 2025 festival, Lil Baby explained that a lack of shoes and school supplies could steer children off track. He also spoke about sparing parents the stress of paying for those things.

He said he is already working on the new approach, but did not announce school partners or a launch date.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Diddy’s Lawyers Want Out After Seven Months Without A Payment
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Diddy's law firm sought to leave another rape case, citing seven months without payment amid his documentary and prison disputes.
item.content:encoded:
Diddy faced another bid by his lawyers to drop him after they told a federal judge he had paid them nothing for more than seven months.

Sher Tremonte LLP asked to withdraw from Thalia Graves’ sexual assault lawsuit in an October 15 filing, extending a fee dispute that had already spilled into other cases. Partner Michael Tremonte also sought permission to hold Diddy’s files until the firm received its money.

The declaration did not disclose the amount owed. It said Diddy, whose legal name is Sean Combs, last paid for work and expenses dating to late 2025.

“More specifically, Mr. Combs has not paid Sher Tremonte anything for over seven months and his last payment related to fees and expenses that were incurred in late 2025. Accordingly, a substantial portion of the total overdue balance consists of invoices that are over 90 days in arrears,” Tremonte wrote.

The firm said the problem went beyond money. Tremonte accused Diddy of refusing the direct talks needed to handle his cases, despite repeated warnings sent to Fort Dix and to the person holding his power of attorney.

“In addition to Mr. Combs’s refusal to pay in accordance with the express terms of his agreement to do so, there has been a total breakdown in cooperation and communication between Mr. Combs and the Firm. Mr. Combs has declined to make himself available for timely, substantive, and direct communications about his cases for over four months,” he wrote.

Graves sued Diddy and Joseph Sherman in September 2024, alleging they drugged and raped her at a New York recording studio in 2001 and recorded the assault. Diddy denied her allegations. Sherman denied ever meeting her.

The new request followed Sher Tremonte’s attempts to leave Diddy’s cases involving producer Lil Rod and NewsNation parent Nexstar. In September, Diddy disputed the firm’s billing through spokesperson Juda Engelmayer, telling USA TODAY that lawyers had charged him for work he never approved. He described the split as a business dispute.

That fight over his own legal bills came as Diddy was also ordered to cover an opponent’s costs in his documentary battle.

On October 6, Judge Phaedra F. Perry-Bond awarded NBCUniversal, Peacock and Ample $477,700.50 after dismissing his lawsuit over Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy. Diddy had sought at least $100 million, alleging the film spread false accusations involving murder and sex with minors. The judge cut the companies’ requested legal bill of $990,292 by more than half.

NBC also put his prison life under scrutiny. Its September investigation cited former fellow inmates who alleged he had access to liquor and banned electronics and paid others for meals, cleaning and massages. His team maintained he was following prison rules.

Union official Jose Rojas told TMZ Diddy’s record listed July 31 and September 30 fights, plus phone violations.

NBC separately reported that prison officials sanctioned him for disruptive conduct and stripped him of 41 days of good-conduct time, citing a union official.

The latest prison controversy also brought a firm denial. The Bureau of Prisons told USA TODAY on October 15 that the reported fight with Christopher “Dudus” Coke did not happen. Engelmayer said Diddy’s team had no verified information that anyone attacked him or that he suffered injuries.

Diddy is serving a 50-month sentence after his convictions on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. He was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking.

In the Graves case, Tremonte argued that replacing counsel would not delay a trial or hearing because the case was stayed while two appeals addressed the law underlying a dismissal argument. The firm asked the judge to approve its exit and let it retain the files until payment.

item.title: Doechii Producer Stoic Isn’t Sold On ’90s Boom-Bap
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Stoic connected his selective boom-bap taste with a simpler studio process and a stronger voice when guiding artists through songs.
item.content:encoded:
Stoic explained why much of 1990s boom-bap left him cold, even as he praised some of the producers who helped shape it.

The producer behind Doechii’s “Bullfrog,” from her Grammy-winning Alligator Bites Never Heal, discussed his taste and growing confidence in a new interview with Hearing Things.

“I’m admittedly not the hugest fan of ’90s boom-bap beats,” he said.

His exceptions included Q-Tip, J Dilla and Madlib. He singled out A Tribe Called Quest’s “Electric Relaxation” for its restrained drums, bassline and uncluttered arrangement.

Stoic also argued No I.D. deserved more consideration in top-10 and even top-five producer conversations. He praised how Jay-Z’s “The Story of O.J.” transformed a sample while giving the rapper something to play against.

The choices accompanied a more assertive approach to his own sessions.

“I feel comfortable being in a room and guiding a song now,” he said, contrasting that confidence with his approach five or six years earlier.

That preference for room inside a beat carried into his own work. Stoic said the project file for “Bullfrog” contained roughly five tracks, with drums, bass and guitar forming its core.

He described keeping the middle of a mix clear for vocals, then placing other sounds around that space. Drums and bass anchored the track while textures and higher sounds gave it color. He had learned to picture a recording room where musicians occupied separate areas, rather than piling every instrument together.

His tools followed the same principle. He limited his main collection to roughly 20 favorite plugins and sounds, allowing him to work with fewer choices and finish tracks more efficiently.

Stoic took the same approach when selecting beats for his producer album PAELLA!. He chose tracks that left enough room for rappers, acknowledging that producers could add too much simply because they enjoyed the process.

His usual method began with a drum break and a sample. After finding and arranging roughly eight to 12 useful pieces, he removed the original break and built his own drums. Bass or guitar could follow.

He also mixed while composing. Rather than relying on an elaborate chain, he said equalization, volume levels and panning accounted for about 95% of his mixing work.
